questions.q: According to the historical description by Clement Dukes in 1900, which of the following clinical features best distinguished 4th disease (Filatov-Dukes) from classic scarlet fever (2nd disease)?
opts: Presence of severe exudative pharyngitis and pathognomonic strawberry tongue
Absence of severe systemic toxicity, extreme high fevers, severe pharyngitis, and strawberry tongue despite a scarlatiniform rash
Longer incubation period (9–21 days) with vesicular rather than maculopapular morphology
Male predominance and race-specific epidemiology in school-aged populations
questions.exp: Dukes clinically distinguished 4th disease by the presence of a bright, generalised, scarlatiniform rash that evolved with fine desquamation, BUT crucially lacked the severe systemic toxicity, extreme fevers, exudative pharyngitis, and strawberry tongue that define classic streptococcal scarlet fever. This mild phenotype with a scarlatiniform rash is now understood to be explained by staphylococcal enterotoxin-mediated superantigen response without severe oropharyngeal involvement.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's grand hall, Dukes spots a RASH THAT LOOKS SCARY (scarlatiniform) BUT has NO SORE THROAT or STRAWBERRY TONGUE—like a wolf in sheep's clothing. The rash ROARS but the MOUTH WHISPERS—that's the missing 'strawberry' that separates 4th from 2nd disease.

questions.q: A 4-month-old girl with incontinentia pigmenti shows complete resolution of her stage 1 vesicular lesions. Histopathology from the acute phase revealed eosinophilic spongiosis with dyskeratotic keratinocytes and peripheral blood eosinophilia. What embryonic principle explains the linear and whorled distribution of her skin findings?
opts: X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) creating functional mosaicism along the lines of Blaschko
Asymmetric migration of neural crest cells during weeks 5–8 of gestation
Randomly activated HLA-B27 responsive dermal dendritic cells
Segmental distribution following the dermatomes of the thoracic and lumbar spinal nerves
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti's characteristic linear and whorled pattern follows the lines of Blaschko, which reflect embryonic X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) patterns. Normal and mutant cells exist in functional mosaicism; targeted apoptosis of mutant keratinocytes creates the distinctive distribution that maps to keratinocyte migration pathways during development. 🏰 Palace: Imagine the castle's throne room split down the middle by LYON'S BLADE (lyonization)—the mutant cells on one side spontaneously combust (apoptosis), leaving BLASCHKO'S BLAZING STRIPES burned into the stone floor.

questions.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with erythematous, edematous dermatitis with scaling and papules on the buttocks, lower abdomen, and medial thighs. The deep inguinal folds and gluteal cleft are notably spared. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this distribution pattern?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes in areas of friction
Primary irritant contact dermatitis from urine, feces, and friction on convex surfaces in direct diaper contact
Candida albicans infection preferentially colonizing skin folds and occluded areas
Genetic atopic diathesis causing selective epidermal barrier deficiency in exposed areas
questions.exp: Primary irritant diaper dermatitis characteristically affects convex surfaces in direct contact with the diaper (buttocks, abdomen, thighs, genitalia) while sparing deep intertriginous areas like the inguinal folds and gluteal cleft, which remain protected from direct irritation. This distribution is driven by physical and chemical irritation from urine, fecal enzymes, and friction rather than infection or autoimmunity.

questions.q: A dermatologist reviews historical literature describing a patient's condition as 'Incontinentia Pigmenti Achromians.' Why is this term now considered a major misnomer and should no longer be used in modern dermatology practice?
opts: The term was never validated by the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) system

Hypomelanosis of Ito is genetically and pathophysiologically unrelated to true Incontinentia Pigmenti, and HI lacks the initial vesicular, blistering, and verrucous inflammatory stages that define true IP
The eponym incorrectly attributes the condition to a specific researcher when it was discovered by multiple teams simultaneously
The term implies a permanent depigmentation pattern, whereas HI presents with transient lesions that resolve spontaneously within 2 years
questions.exp:
Although historically Hypomelanosis of Ito was called 'Incontinentia Pigmenti Achromians' because it appeared as a negative image of true Incontinentia Pigmenti (Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome), this is a fundamental misnomer. HI is completely genetically and pathophysiologically distinct from true IP and critically lacks the characteristic initial vesicular, blistering, and verrucous inflammatory stages that define true Incontinentia Pigmenti. The two conditions are unrelated neurocutaneous disorders.
🏰 Palace: Picture a NEGATIVE PHOTO DARKROOM where two COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PATIENTS are displayed—one is BLISTERED and VERRUCOUS (true IP bursting with inflammation), the other is just PALE and CALM (HI with mosaicism)—never confuse the PHOTO NEGATIVE TRICK with genetic KINSHIP.

questions.q: A 19-year-old girl is diagnosed with a Reed nevus on dermoscopy. Which of the following demographic and clinical features are most consistent with this diagnosis?
opts: Prepubertal presentation with male predominance and predilection for facial lesions
Second to third decade of life with female predominance (2:1 ratio) and thigh as most common site
Older adults over age 50 with symmetric distribution across trunk and extremities
Infants under age 5 with rapid growth that does not stabilize and preference for flexural areas
questions.exp: Reed nevus shows a distinct predilection for young adults in the second to third decade of life with a marked female predominance (2:1 female-to-male ratio). Approximately 67% of lesions occur on the extremities, overwhelmingly favoring the thighs of young women. This demographic pattern distinguishes Reed nevus from classic pink Spitz nevi which heavily target prepubertal children.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a bizarre, angular patch of alopecia on the frontoparietal scalp. His mother reports he unconsciously pulls his hair while watching cartoons. Dermoscopy shows hair shaft fracturing (trichoclasis) without significant perifollicular inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis and key differentiating feature from alopecia areata?
opts: Trichotillomania; strict absence of perifollicular inflammation due to mechanical trauma pathogenesis
Alopecia areata; presence of trichoclasis and trichomalacia on dermoscopy
Androgenetic alopecia; bimodal age of onset with male predominance in childhood
Telogen effluvium; associated with obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorders
questions.exp: Trichotillomania is a self-induced mechanical trauma disorder (not autoimmune), so it lacks the characteristic perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation seen in alopecia areata. The trichoclasis and trichomalacia result from repetitive traction force on the hair shaft and bulb, not immune destruction. The absence of autoantibodies and HLA associations further distinguishes it from autoimmune alopecias.

questions.q: A 2-week-old female infant presents with crops of tense vesicles and bullae in a linear, whorled distribution affecting the extremities and trunk. Her mother reports lesions were present at birth. Which genetic defect and molecular mechanism underlie this presentation?
opts: IKBKG gene mutation preventing NF-κB pathway activation, leading to TNF-α-induced apoptosis of mutant keratinocytes
COL17A1 mutation causing autoimmune-mediated basement membrane destruction
LAMB3 mutation resulting in junctional epidermolysis bullosa simplex
DSP mutation causing desmosomal protein deficiency with acantholysis
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti is caused by IKBKG (NEMO) gene mutations on Xq28, which prevent proper NF-κB pathway activation. Without this protective pathway, mutant keratinocytes undergo spontaneous apoptosis in response to TNF-α. The condition is X-linked dominant and predominantly affects females due to embryonic lethality in males. 🏰 Palace: Picture a NEMO fish trapped in a castle dungeon (IKBKG mutation) unable to activate the NF-κB bouncer (guard) protecting against TNF-α assassins stabbing cells to death.

questions.q: A 6-month-old girl with confirmed Sturge-Weber syndrome presents with a port-wine stain involving the left ophthalmic distribution (V1). Neuroimaging reveals ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis. Which embryological origin best explains why the facial capillary malformation, leptomeningeal involvement, and choroidal malformation are typically ipsilateral?
opts: The GNAQ mutation occurs in dorsal root ganglion cells after neural tube closure
The mutation arises very early in the anterior neural crest/cephalic mesenchyme before widespread migration, affecting the clonal derivatives populating the frontonasal prominence
Vascular endothelial cells from the pharyngeal arches carry the mutation to multiple sites independently
The mutation occurs in the notochord, which induces symmetrical vascular malformations
questions.exp:
The somatic GNAQ mutation in SWS occurs very early during embryogenesis within the anterior neural crest or cephalic mesenchyme, before widespread neural crest migration. The mutant clone then populates the frontonasal prominence, whose neural-crest derivatives form the upper facial cutaneous vasculature, leptomeninges overlying the ipsilateral cortex, and the ocular choroid—explaining the simultaneous ipsilateral involvement of all three components.
🏰 Palace: Imagine the NEURAL CREST as a ROYAL COURIER who receives a DEFECTIVE LETTER (GNAQ mutation) early in his journey at the castle gates—he then delivers copies to three different wings of the same castle (face, brain, eye), all on the SAME SIDE of the castle.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy with neurofibromatosis type 1 presents with multiple scattered papules consistent with juvenile xanthogranuloma. What is the approximate increased risk of developing juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia in this patient compared to the general pediatric population?
opts: 2 to 5-fold increased risk
20 to 30-fold increased risk
50 to 75-fold increased risk
100-fold increased risk
questions.exp: The 'Triple Association' is a high-yield exam concept: children with both Neurofibromatosis type 1 and cutaneous JXG have a 20 to 30-fold increased risk of developing Juvenile Myelomonocytic Leukemia, likely due to shared RAS pathway hyperactivity in the context of NF1-driven NF1 haploinsufficiency.
questions.🏰 Palace: Picture a TRIPLE-STACKED PYRAMID in the castle: NF1 + JXG = 20–30× JMML RISK, each level representing exponential danger lurking in the RAS pathway corridors beneath the castle.

questions.q: A 13-year-old male with Becker's nevus shows a sudden increase in hypertrichosis and development of acneiform lesions confined to the hyperpigmented patch over the past 6 months. Which hormonal receptor is directly responsible for triggering these adolescent changes?
opts: Androgen receptor with increased density and activity in lesional skin
Estrogen receptor-alpha promoting sebaceous gland differentiation
Growth hormone receptor causing generalized pilosebaceous hyperplasia
Thyroid hormone receptor regulating melanin synthesis
questions.exp: The clinical evolution of Becker's nevus during puberty is uniquely driven by localized heightened sensitivity to circulating androgens, with documented increase in the density and activity of androgen receptors within the lesional skin. This androgen-receptor stimulation triggers both hypertrichosis and acneiform lesions, which are strictly limited to the area of hyperpigmentation.

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl presents with asymmetric hypopigmented streaks following the lines of Blaschko on her trunk and extremities. Her parents report developmental delay and mild intellectual disability. Which of the following best characterizes the pathophysiological basis of Hypomelanosis of Ito?
opts: Autoimmune attack on melanocytes mediated by HLA-associated pathogenic antibodies
Post-zygotic somatic mutation in early embryogenesis leading to a clone of pigment-deficient skin cells
Immune-complex deposition in the basement membrane zone causing melanocyte destruction
Inherited germline mutation with autosomal dominant transmission affecting melanin biosynthesis
questions.exp:
Hypomelanosis of Ito is a genetic mosaicism resulting from post-zygotic somatic mutations occurring early in embryogenesis, creating clones of melanocytes with decreased pigment synthesis. It is NOT autoimmune, does not involve HLA associations, pathogenic antibodies, or immune-complex mechanisms. The condition is driven by chromosomal mosaicisms detectable in lymphocytes or cultured lesional fibroblasts.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a CLONE ARMY of defective MELANIN WORKERS being assembled in an EARLY EMBRYONIC FACTORY (post-zygotic), building PALE BUILDINGS (hypopigmentation) along BLASCHKO'S BLUEPRINTS in the castle's trunk and tower.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with poorly defined, round hypopigmented macules covered with fine white scale on his cheeks that fail to tan in summer. Histology shows follicular plugging, follicular spongiosis, and atrophic sebaceous glands. Which mechanism best explains the hypopigmentation in pityriasis alba?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes via anti-tyrosinase antibodies
Low-grade eczematous dermatitis disrupting melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes, and possible tyrosinase inhibition by Malassezia metabolites or copper deficiency
Complete loss of melanocyte function due to HLA-associated genetic predisposition
Epidermal barrier dysfunction leading to increased transepidermal water loss and secondary melanin degradation
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is fundamentally a low-grade localized eczema causing post-inflammatory hypopigmentation through disruption of melanosome transfer. The pathogenesis does not involve specific autoantigen-autoantibody complexes or HLA haplotypes. Dicarboxylic acids from Malassezia and low copper levels inhibit tyrosinase activity.

questions.q: A 8-month-old boy presents with a single 1.5 cm dome-shaped nodule on his neck. Histopathology shows dermal infiltration with cells positive for CD68 and Factor XIIIa, but negative for CD1a and Langerin. Which genetic alteration is most characteristically associated with this diagnosis?
opts: BRAF V600E mutation
CSF1R mutations or NTRK1 fusions
TP53 germline mutation
PTEN loss-of-function mutation
questions.exp: Juvenile Xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis enriched for somatic kinase-activating alterations, specifically CSF1R mutations (10%) and NTRK1 fusions (12%), distinguishing it from Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis which carries BRAF V600E. The CD1a-negative, Langerin-negative immunophenotype with CD68+ dermal dendrocytes confirms JXG rather than LCH.
questions.🏰 Palace: Imagine CSF1R and NTRK1 mutations as two GOLDEN KEYS locked in a JUVENILE XANTHOGRANULOMA CASTLE, while BRAF V600E (the villain) batters the gates of the rival LCH fortress next door.

questions.q: A 14-month-old with severe, long-standing diaper dermatitis develops multiple reddish-purplish nodules (0.5–3 cm) on the convexities of the diaper area. Histopathology reveals a dense, mixed dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils. What is the correct histological diagnosis?
opts: True epithelioid granulomas consistent with tuberculosis or sarcoidosis
Granuloma Gluteale Infantum—despite its name, showing hyperplastic inflammation without true granulomatous architecture
Jacquet's erosive diaper dermatitis with full-thickness epidermal ulceration
Candida-specific microabscess formation within the stratum corneum
questions.exp: Granuloma Gluteale Infantum is a misnomer; histopathology definitively lacks true granulomas and instead shows a dense, mixed inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils representing a hyperplastic tissue reaction to irritants, Candida, or inappropriate potent topical corticosteroid use. The clinical presentation of violaceous nodules on the diaper area is distinctive, but the histology does not support a granulomatous process.

questions.q: Pigmentary mosaicism represents a group of genetically determined conditions arising from somatic postzygotic mutations. Which of the following statements accurately reflects the pathogenesis of these conditions?
opts: They are caused by autoimmune-mediated destruction of melanocytes with documented autoantibody isotypes and HLA associations
They result from inherited germline mutations inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high penetrance
They are strictly sporadic conditions caused by postzygotic somatic chromosomal alterations occurring early in embryogenesis, with over 90% of aberrations overlapping with pigmentation genes
They arise from inflammatory cytokine cascades triggered by specific immune receptors targeting dermal fibroblasts
questions.exp: Pigmentary mosaicism conditions result from postzygotic somatic mutations occurring early in embryogenesis, making them strictly sporadic and not inherited. Over 90% of chromosomal aberrations overlap with known pigmentation genes. These conditions completely lack autoimmune or inflammatory mechanisms, antibody isotypes, HLA associations, or targeted inflammatory cytokine cascades—they are purely developmental and structural anomalies.

questions.q: A 2-week-old infant presents with widespread, asymptomatic streaky brown macules distributed in a V-shaped pattern on the back and S-shaped bands on the chest, following embryonic migration pathways. On histology, increased melanin is noted strictly within basal keratinocytes with normal melanocyte numbers and no dermal melanophages. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
opts: Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis (LWNH)
Hypomelanosis of Ito
Incontinentia Pigmenti
Segmental neurofibromatosis type 1
questions.exp: LWNH presents in the first few weeks of life with diffuse, asymptomatic streaky hyperpigmented macules following Blaschko's lines. The key histological finding is epidermal melanotic hypermelanosis (increased melanin in basal keratinocytes) with normal melanocyte numbers and importantly, no dermal melanophages or pigment incontinence. This distinguishes it from Incontinentia Pigmenti, which shows pigment incontinence.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a solitary, dark brown-black papule measuring 4 mm on her thigh that appeared over the past 6 months. Dermoscopy reveals a diffuse dark center with radiating pigmented streaks in a symmetric pattern. Which histological layer is characteristically affected in a classic Reed nevus?
opts: Predominantly junctional, confined to the dermal-epidermal junction and superficial papillary dermis, sparing the deep reticular dermis
Full-thickness involvement extending from epidermis through the deep reticular dermis into subcutaneous fat
Exclusively intraepidermal with no dermal component
Primarily deep reticular dermal proliferation with minimal junctional involvement
questions.exp: Reed nevus is a predominantly junctional melanocytic proliferation strictly confined to the dermal-epidermal junction and superficial papillary dermis, characteristically sparing the deep reticular dermis. The spindle-shaped melanocytes may proliferate downward into the papillary dermis but remain within these superficial layers, distinguishing it histologically from deeper dermal nevi. This restricted anatomic involvement is a key diagnostic criterion.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with progressive nail dystrophy, reticulate gray-brown hyperpigmentation on the chest and neck, and oral leukoplakia on the tongue. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the DKC1 gene at Xq28. Which of the following best explains the molecular pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: Autoimmune attack on nail matrix antigens mediated by pathogenic IgG antibodies
Mutations in telomere maintenance genes leading to critically shortened telomeres and premature cellular senescence
HLA-associated immune complex deposition in the basement membrane zone
Defective melanin synthesis due to tyrosinase gene mutations
questions.exp: Dyskeratosis congenita is a primary genetic disorder of telomere biology caused by mutations in genes encoding telomerase complex proteins and shelterin proteins (such as DKC1, which encodes dyskerin). These mutations result in critically shortened telomeres, leading to premature cellular senescence and apoptosis in rapidly dividing cells. The disease is NOT autoimmune, immunobullous, or mediated by pathogenic antibodies or HLA associations.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with a mild febrile illness, generalised scarlatiniform rash, and fine desquamation. Notably, there is an absence of severe pharyngitis and strawberry tongue. What is the modern medical consensus regarding this clinical presentation historically described as 4th disease (Filatov-Dukes)?
opts: It represents a distinct disease entity caused by a specific fourth pathogenic organism
It is an obsolete diagnosis now explained by staphylococcal scarlatiniform erythroderma or atypical viral exanthems
It is pathognomonic for Group A Streptococcus with an unusually mild phenotype
It requires specific HLA associations and a unique histopathological pattern for diagnosis
questions.exp: Fourth disease (Filatov-Dukes) is no longer recognised as a distinct disease entity in modern medicine. The historical clinical picture—scarlatiniform rash with absence of severe pharyngitis and strawberry tongue—is now understood to represent either staphylococcal superantigen-mediated erythroderma or mild viral exanthems that were not molecularly differentiated in the early 1900s.
questions.memory_palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine Dukes' ghost in the castle library discovering that his prized 'Fourth Disease' manuscript is actually a BLANK BOOK—because 4th disease is OBSOLETE and never existed as a true entity. The scarlatiniform rash was always just Staph or viral pretenders wearing a costume.

questions.q: A 15-year-old girl with major depression and anxiety presents with areas of scalp reduced to coarse stubble. She admits to consciously identifying hairs as feeling 'coarse' or 'out of place' and compulsively removing them. She also confesses to chewing and swallowing the plucked hair. Which complication should you screen for most urgently?
opts: Trichobezoar formation leading to potential gastrointestinal obstruction (Rapunzel syndrome)
Development of scarring alopecia due to chronic perifollicular inflammation
HLA-associated autoimmune thyroiditis due to shared genetic predisposition
Secondary bacterial infection with subsequent cellulitis and sepsis
questions.exp: Trichophagia (chewing and swallowing plucked hair) is a serious complication of trichotillomania that can lead to trichobezoar formation—an intestinal hairball that may cause life-threatening gastrointestinal obstruction (Rapunzel syndrome). This represents the most urgent medical complication requiring screening in patients who admit to hair ingestion. Trichotillomania does not cause scarring alopecia or autoimmune sequelae.

questions.q: Which of the following is the key distinguishing feature differentiating extensive pityriasis alba from classic pityriasis alba?
opts: Extensive variant shows erythematous patches that never resolve, whereas classic PA resolves within 2 weeks

Extensive variant presents in teenagers and young adults with widespread lesions exceeding 2 cm diameter on trunk and limbs, whereas classic PA favors facial involvement in children with smaller lesions
Extensive variant is caused by autoimmune mechanisms, whereas classic PA is purely post-inflammatory
Extensive variant demonstrates sebaceous gland hyperplasia on histology, whereas classic PA shows sebaceous gland atrophy
questions.exp: The extensive variant of pityriasis alba affects teenagers and young adults with female predominance and presents with widespread, larger patches (>2 cm) on trunk and limbs. Classic pityriasis alba occurs in children with facial predominance and smaller lesions (0.5–3 cm). Both share the same pathophysiology but differ in epidemiology and distribution.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with pruritic, flat-topped purple papules on his wrists and ankles that exhibit new lesions in lines of trauma. Which immune cell type is primarily responsible for the direct cytotoxic attack on basal keratinocytes in lichen planus?
opts: CD4+ helper T-cells only
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes
B-cells producing pathogenic IgG autoantibodies
CD19+ plasma cells secreting IgA
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disorder with NO pathogenic autoantibodies (direct immunofluorescence is negative or non-specific). CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes are recruited by NK cells via CXCR-3 ligands and directly attack basal keratinocytes at the dermoepidermal junction. CD4+ helper T-cells play a supporting role in the dermis, but CD8+ Tc cells are the primary effectors.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a WARRIOR (CD8) stabbing the CASTLE FOUNDATION (basal layer) with a glowing blue sword (cytotoxic granules), while a GHOST KING (CD4) watches from the shadows—the ghost cannot touch, only CD8 can.

questions.q: A pregnant woman with systemic lupus erythematosus carrying anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies delivers a neonate. Which fetal cardiac structure is the primary target of transplacental IgG antibodies in neonatal lupus?
opts: Left ventricular wall
Atrioventricular node
Pulmonary valve
Right atrial appendage
questions.exp: Cardiac neonatal lupus involves permanent injury (unlike transient cutaneous manifestations) occurring in 61% of isolated NLE cases. Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies specifically target L-type calcium channels on fetal cardiomyocytes and the atrioventricular node, resulting in potentially fatal congenital complete atrioventricular block. 🏰 Palace: Imagine a WINDING CASTLE CORRIDOR (AVN—atrioventricular node) where maternal ANTIBODIES as guards BLOCK the calcium channel gates, stopping the HEART RHYTHM like a broken hourglass.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with a well-demarcated, irregularly bordered tan-brown patch on his right shoulder that has progressively enlarged over the past 2 years with coarse dark terminal hairs erupting from the surface. Which genetic mutation is primarily responsible for the pathogenesis of this lesion?
opts: Postzygotic somatic mutations in the ACTB gene affecting pilar smooth muscle cells
Germline mutations in the KIT gene with autosomal dominant inheritance
Loss-of-function mutations in the PTEN gene causing hamartomatous growth
Gain-of-function mutations in the BRAF gene similar to Spitz nevi
questions.exp: Becker's nevus is driven by postzygotic somatic mutations in the ACTB gene (encoding beta-actin) that potentiate Hedgehog pathway signaling and disrupt hair follicle development. These mutations are specifically located within pilar smooth muscle cells of the lesional area and cause mosaic inheritance rather than germline transmission.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with X-linked dyskeratosis congenita (Zinsser-Cole-Engman syndrome) develops pancytopenia and bone marrow failure. What is the approximate percentage of DKC patients who develop bone marrow failure as a life-threatening complication?
opts: Up to 30% of patients
Up to 60% of patients
Up to 90% of patients
Up to 15% of patients
questions.exp: Up to 90% of dyskeratosis congenita patients develop bone marrow failure (pancytopenia/aplastic anemia), which accounts for approximately 70% of mortality in this condition. This makes hematologic failure the primary cause of early death in DKC, despite the characteristic cutaneous features being the initial diagnostic clues.

questions.q: What is the peak age of onset for childhood lichen planus, and in which population does it account for up to 20% of all lichen planus cases?
opts: 2–4 years of age; African Americans
8–12 years of age; Pacific Indians
14–16 years of age; Middle Eastern populations
5–7 years of age; Indian subcontinent
questions.exp: Childhood lichen planus is rare overall (1–5% of total LP cases) and peaks between 8 and 12 years of age. Pacific Indians have the highest prevalence, accounting for up to 20% of cases in that population, with frequent reports also from the Indian subcontinent, Middle East, and African American children.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Eight to Twelve year olds dress as PACIFIC ISLANDERS (wearing grass skirts) in the castle courtyard—they make up the TWENTY-PERCENT royal guard, the most elite squad protecting the throne room.

questions.q: A 2-month-old boy presents with a deep-purple facial capillary malformation (port-wine stain) over the left V1 and V2 distribution. His parents ask about inheritance risk for future children. Which genetic mechanism best explains the inheritance pattern of Sturge-Weber syndrome?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance
Somatic postzygotic GNAQ mutation causing mosaic disease; no germline transmission
X-linked recessive inheritance with male predominance
Autosomal recessive inheritance requiring two mutated alleles
questions.exp:
Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder caused by a postzygotic somatic activating missense mutation in GNAQ (c.548G>A; p.Arg183Gln) that occurs early in embryogenesis within the anterior neural crest. Because the defect is somatic and mosaic (present only in lesional tissue, not germline), there is no germline transmission and affected individuals do not pass the condition to offspring.
🏰 Palace: Picture a MOSAIC TILE FLOOR where only SOME tiles (somatic cells) are cracked after the builder started—the blueprint (germline) was never defective, so the next house built from the same blueprint will be perfect.

questions.q: A 6-week-old neonate presents with erythematous, arcuate lesions on the face and periorbital areas. The mother has a positive anti-Ro/SSA serologic profile. Which autoantibody is present in >90% of cases of cutaneous neonatal lupus?
opts: Anti-La/SSB
Anti-Ro/SSA
Anti-U1-RNP
Anti-centromere
questions.exp: Cutaneous neonatal lupus erythematosus (CNLE) is characterized by maternal IgG1 autoantibodies directed against ribonucleoproteins, with anti-Ro/SSA present in >90% of cases, followed less commonly by anti-La/SSB and anti-U1-RNP. The characteristic 'owl eyes' or 'raccoon eyes' appearance occurs due to periorbital lesion confluence. 🏰 Palace: Picture a WISE OWL wearing ROE (fish eggs/Ro-SSA) as spectacles, peering from the castle tower at 90% success rate.
